% ---------------------------------------------------------------- [A] abstract (replacement)
Validation on our own simulator uses a continuous 15-minute schedule and an adopted
$0.02$~mag detectability floor, so the numbers above are benchmark values rather than \Rom{}
yield forecasts. On an independent simulation of the survey as planned (GULLS, RMDC26 release;
$\bmlGullsN$ matched events never used in training), the shipped checkpoint fails on the
schedule's seven mid-season pauses, flagging $\bmlGullsFaShippedPct\%$ of single lenses as
anomalous; a gap-aware, finite-source fine-tune of the same network, trained only on our own
simulations, brings that to $\bmlGullsFaFsplPct\%$ at the same threshold and nearly doubles
planetary recall at a matched false-alarm budget ($\bmlGullsRecShippedAtBudget \rightarrow
\bmlGullsRecFsplAtBudget$ at $\bmlGullsBudgetPct\%$). Applying our labelling policy to the
independent simulation's noise-free curves shows that $\bmlGullsUndetPct\%$ of its ``planetary''
events carry no anomaly a survey could claim, which bounds any recall quoted against generator
labels. Code, weights, and reproducibility artifacts are released openly.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------- [B] Sec. limits, replacement paragraph
\paragraph{The schedule, not the sampling rate, is what the shipped model cannot survive.}
Our training grid is continuous within a season. The survey as planned is not: the GBTDS
schedule implemented in the RMDC26 release pauses F146 seven times per 70.7-day season for
$\sim$6~h, at fixed season phases, and the season itself is 1.3 days shorter than our 72-day
window. Not one of our training events contains an empty mid-season bin, so the model's only
prior for an empty token is the unrevealed future of a truncated season. Inserting the seven
pauses into our own held-out events, with nothing else changed, collapses the shipped model
(Table~\ref{tab:gap}): single-lens recall falls from $\bmlGapShippedPsplClean$ to
$\bmlGapShippedPsplSched$ and \texttt{Flat} recall to $\bmlGapShippedFlatSched$, both going to
\texttt{NonPSPL} and \texttt{PeriodicVar}, while the anomaly and variable classes are unaffected.
Gaps of $\le 2$~h are harmless. The remedy is an augmentation, not a new model: blanking one to
eight contiguous runs of 1--12~h in every band during a warm-start fine-tune of the shipped
weights (12 epochs, relabelling by what survives) restores held-out macro-F1 under the schedule
from $\bmlGapShippedF1Sched$ to $\bmlGapAwareF1Sched$ at a clean-data cost of
$\bmlGapAwareF1CleanDelta$. Training on the \emph{exact} schedule instead of a distribution over
gaps does slightly better still on our own simulations ($\bmlGapSchedApSched$ versus
$\bmlGapRandApSched$ average precision), but does not transfer better (\S\ref{sec:gulls}), and
exposes the coarse onset grid of \S\ref{sec:sims} as a hazard: under a fixed mask two of the ten
onset values fall inside the blanked bins and the caustic-in-gap relabel then mislabels
$\bmlGapRelabelPct\%$ of all binaries. The released checkpoints were trained on that grid; the
generator now resolves the onset at $0.5$~d. The multi-season structure is addressed
in \S\ref{sec:gulls}. The shipped checkpoint's input contract is therefore \emph{continuous
F146}; for the planned schedule, the gap-aware checkpoint is the one to use.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------- [C] new section
\section{Cross-simulator validation on an independent \Rom{} simulation}\label{sec:gulls}

Every number so far comes from our own simulator, so every number so far could in principle
reflect our simulator rather than the sky. The Roman Galactic Exoplanet Survey Project
Infrastructure Team's RMDC26 release \citep{RGESPIT2026} is a simulation of the survey as
currently planned, produced with GULLS \citep{Penny2019} by a different group, with the planned
schedule, the planned exposure and calibration, and a Galactic population we did not choose. We
use it as a test set. No event from it entered training, no threshold was chosen on it, and no
event was excluded on the basis of the model's output.

\subsection{Data, selection, and input contract}

RMDC26 contains 385{,}004 events in three classes: single lenses (1S1L), planetary lenses
(1S2L), and planetary lenses with a binary source (2S2L). Two facts about the classes matter for
reading the results. First, 2S2L is \emph{not} the binary-source contaminant of
\S\ref{sec:sims}: its planet mass-ratio distribution is identical to 1S2L's (median
$q = 1.25\times10^{-4}$), so every 2S2L event carries a genuine planetary anomaly and the binary
source is an additional complication in 56\% of them. A \texttt{NonPSPL} call on 2S2L is
substantially correct. RMDC26 ships no pure binary-source class, so the \citet{Gaudi1998}
degeneracy raised in \S\ref{sec:discussion} remains untested here. Second, the planetary
population is harder than ours at matched amplitude: the median $q$ is a factor of several below
our prior's, and the amplitude selection below keeps faint perturbations. The
transfer recall is therefore not comparable to the in-distribution completeness of
\S\ref{sec:results}.

Selection is on inputs, applied identically to all three classes. We keep events whose
metadata-derived peak amplitude exceeds $0.1$~mag (GULLS simulates the whole population,
including events no survey would register: the median single-lens amplitude is $0.063$~mag),
whose Einstein timescale lies inside our training prior's support ($1 \le t_{\rm E} \le 300$~d;
RMDC26's single-lens class is 33\% sub-day events, a free-floating-planet-like population
that BinML was never asked to handle, whereas its binary classes are 0.2\% sub-day), and whose
peak falls inside one of the six high-cadence seasons. That leaves $\bmlGullsEligibleN$ eligible
events, of which $\bmlGullsN$ are scored; the rest have their peak between seasons
($\bmlGullsGapPct\%$) or in one of the four low-cadence seasons ($\bmlGullsLowcadPct\%$), and we
return to them in \S\ref{sec:gulls:seasons}. The model is given the 72-day window starting at
the season boundary in all three bands, with the baseline measured from the data (the median
F146 magnitude more than $5\,t_{\rm E}$ from the peak over the full mission, as a survey pipeline
would have), because the catalogue baseline in this release is offset from the observed
quiescent flux. Observations are pooled to one value per 15-minute epoch before binning, exactly
as the training cache is built, so the 12.1-minute cadence is indistinguishable from ours after
preprocessing.

\subsection{Results}

Table~\ref{tab:gulls} gives the single-lens false-alarm rate at the frozen operating threshold
and planetary recall at matched false-alarm budgets, on the identical $\bmlGullsN$ events for
every checkpoint. The matched-budget comparison is the one a threshold shift cannot fake. The
shipped checkpoint fails as \S\ref{sec:limits} predicts: $\bmlGullsFaShippedPct\%$ of single
lenses are flagged, and the argmax class for most of them is \texttt{PeriodicVar}, the
signature of the empty mid-season tokens. The gap-aware fine-tune brings this to
$\bmlGullsFaGapawarePct\%$. Its residual false alarms are not random: they rise monotonically
with $\rho/|u_0|$, the ratio of source radius to impact parameter
(Table~\ref{tab:gulls}, last columns), from $\bmlGullsFaGapawareRhoLo$ for point-like sources
to $\bmlGullsFaGapawareRhoHi$ for sources larger than the impact parameter. The cause is in our
generator: the single-lens class was point-source while the binary class sampled a finite
source, so a finite-source single lens, whose rounded peak is unlike any training PSPL, was
read as anomalous. Adding finite-source single lenses to the generator (VBBinaryLensing's
extended-source magnification, $\rho$ drawn up to 5 to cover the GULLS population, binaries
unchanged) and repeating the same 12-epoch fine-tune brings the false-alarm rate to
$\bmlGullsFaFsplPct\%$ and the finite-source bins to $\bmlGullsFaFsplRhoHi$, while planetary
recall at the $\bmlGullsBudgetPct\%$ budget rises from $\bmlGullsRecShippedAtBudget$ (shipped)
through $\bmlGullsRecGapawareAtBudget$ to $\bmlGullsRecFsplAtBudget$. Widening the
\emph{binary} source-size prior at the same time did not help and slightly hurt; the gain is
attributable to the single-lens extension alone. Three other remedies were tested and are
reported because they failed: training on the exact schedule rather than random gaps matches the
random-gap arm at every budget on GULLS; matching GULLS' noise model (its F146 errors equal
ours for sources brighter than 20th magnitude and reach $2.6\times$ ours at 24--25 mag, a
sevenfold background rather than a global factor) is worse on every measure, because the extra
faint-end scatter teaches the model to discount exactly the small deviations the finite-source
extension taught it to read; and the colour bands help rather than hurt, adding
$\bmlGullsColourGain$ to planetary recall at the matched budget for every checkpoint despite
GULLS' different blending and calibration.

\subsection{What ``recall'' means across two label ontologies}\label{sec:gulls:labels}

GULLS labels events by generator: every 1S2L event is ``planetary'' whether or not the planet
leaves a trace. BinML's classes are observational (\S\ref{sec:detcond}). RMDC26 ships the
noise-free light curve and the per-epoch error of every event, so the two ontologies can be
reconciled directly: we applied our own labelling rule, the $\Delta\chi^2$ thresholds and the
$0.02$~mag floor against the best-fitting single-lens model on the noise-free curve, with GULLS'
own errors as $\sigma$, to $\bmlGullsTruthN$ events. Under that rule $\bmlGullsUndet1S2LPct\%$
of 1S2L and $\bmlGullsUndet2S2LPct\%$ of 2S2L events carry no detectable anomaly:
$\bmlGullsUndetChiPct\%$ fail the $\Delta\chi^2$ cut outright and $\bmlGullsUndetFloorPct\%$ pass
it but fall under the amplitude floor. The generator-label recall ceiling is therefore about
$0.56$, not $1$. On binaries whose anomaly is detectable, the finite-source checkpoint's recall
at the frozen threshold is $\bmlGullsRecDet1S2L$ / $\bmlGullsRecDet2S2L$ (1S2L / 2S2L) against
$\bmlGullsRecGen1S2L$ / $\bmlGullsRecGen2S2L$ on generator labels, and it is amplitude-limited:
$\bmlGullsRecAmpLo$ of detectable anomalies of 0.02--0.05~mag are caught, $\bmlGullsRecAmpHi$ of
those above 0.5~mag. The rule also exposes the floor as the binding modelling choice: the model
flags $\bmlGullsFloorFlagPct\%$ of the binaries whose anomaly is statistically significant but
below $0.02$~mag, against $\bmlGullsFaFsplPct\%$ of single lenses. Whether those are false
alarms is exactly the question the floor's justification in \S\ref{sec:detcond} leaves open.

\subsection{Events whose peak falls between seasons}\label{sec:gulls:seasons}

The single-season input contract discards $\bmlGullsGapPct\%$ of the eligible RMDC26 events,
those whose peak falls in one of the 109--120-day gaps between seasons (the mission observes 685
of 1{,}717 days). To measure what that costs without retraining, we scored every high-cadence
season adjacent to the gap for $\bmlGullsMsN$ such events per class and took the maximum anomaly
probability across them, applying the labelling rule of \S\ref{sec:gulls:labels} per season. A
high-cadence adjacent season exists for $\bmlGullsMsScorable1S1L\%$ / $\bmlGullsMsScorable1S2L\%$
/ $\bmlGullsMsScorable2S2L\%$ of the 1S1L / 1S2L / 2S2L events (the remainder border the four
low-cadence seasons). In those wings a detectable anomaly is visible for
$\bmlGullsMsDet1S2L\%$ / $\bmlGullsMsDet2S2L\%$ of the planetary events, against
$\bmlGullsInSeasonDet1S2L\%$ / $\bmlGullsInSeasonDet2S2L\%$ in-season: the schedule itself, not the
model, hides about half of these planets, whose anomaly sits in the unobserved gap. On the
recoverable part the finite-source checkpoint flags $\bmlGullsMsFaPct\%$ of single lenses (a
wing without a peak reads as a single lens or as nothing) and recovers
$\bmlGullsMsRecAt2$ / $\bmlGullsMsRecAt5$ of the wing-detectable anomalies at the 2\% / 5.2\%
budgets, against $\bmlGullsRecDetAtBudget$ in-season. A whole-mission model would not recover the
anomalies that fall in the gap; what it would uniquely add is events spanning seasons and the
four low-cadence seasons ($\bmlGullsLowcadPct\%$ of eligible events, outside BinML's support).

\subsection{The cascade on an independent simulation}\label{sec:gulls:cascade}

The partial-light-curve protocol of \S\ref{sec:cascade} was repeated on $\bmlGullsCascN$ RMDC26
seasons from the same cache: 144 half-day cuts, the first threshold crossing as the alert, and
the truth-informed onset recomputed at every cut on the noise-free curve by our own rule, with
GULLS' errors as $\sigma$. Eligibility is as before (binary lens, anomaly detectable over the
full window, finite onset; $\bmlGullsCascElig$ events), and nothing is selected on the model's
output. Under the primary protocol (F146 only, frozen threshold) the finite-source checkpoint
alerts prematurely on $\bmlGullsCascPrematurePct\%$ of eligible binaries (95\% CI
$[\bmlGullsCascPrematureLo, \bmlGullsCascPrematureHi]\%$; in-house $\bmlCascPrematurePct\%$)
with a median non-premature lag of $\bmlGullsCascLag$~days (in-house
$\bmlCascMedianLagNonPrem$), so the timing behaviour transfers; within-season detection is
lower, $\bmlGullsCascDetPct\%$ against $\bmlCascDetFrac\%$, because the eligible GULLS anomalies
are smaller at matched selection. What the in-house scan could not give is the burden on the
dominant class: $\bmlGullsCascFaSeasonPct\%$ of single lenses alert at least once per season
($\bmlGullsCascFaPerDay$ alerts per 1{,}000 events per day; $\bmlGullsCascFaSeasonCalPct\%$ at the
calibrated threshold), so at a planetary prevalence of 1\% a streaming alert list would be
$\bmlGullsCascPurityOnePct\%$ detectable planets, and $\bmlGullsCascPurityFivePct\%$ at 5\%.
That is the quantitative form of the conclusion in \S\ref{sec:cascade}: the latency and purity
support post-hoc modelling priority, not real-time triggering.

\subsection{Sensitivity to the detectability floor, on the label side}\label{sec:gulls:floor}

Because the noise-free statistics of every relabelled event are stored, the adopted
$0.02$~mag floor can be swept without re-simulation. The fraction of RMDC26 planetary events
with a claimable anomaly is $\bmlGullsFloorDetLo\%$ at a $0.005$~mag floor,
$\bmlGullsFloorDetAdopted\%$ at the adopted $0.02$, and $\bmlGullsFloorDetHi\%$ at $0.05$; the
checkpoint's precision under the resulting labels is highest, $\bmlGullsFloorPrecLo$, at the
lowest floor and falls to $\bmlGullsFloorPrecAdopted$ at $0.02$. The model, trained under the
$0.02$~mag policy, nonetheless detects a class of small but statistically significant anomalies
that the policy declines to claim; whether a survey would claim them is the red-noise question
the floor stands in for (\S\ref{sec:detcond}). The training side of the sensitivity, retraining
under another floor, is not covered here.

\subsection{What this test does and does not establish}

It establishes that the failure of the shipped model on the planned schedule is a property of
the schedule, reproducible with no GULLS data, and remediable by augmentation; that the
remaining transfer gap was a specific missing piece of physics in our generator, found by
diagnosis rather than by tuning; and that our three-band design and our labelling policy
survive contact with an independent population. It does not establish a \Rom{} planet yield:
RMDC26's planetary population is harder than our prior's, the amplitude selection is ours, and
no real-data systematics are present in either simulator. It also does not test the
binary-source degeneracy, for which RMDC26 has no class. Sub-day single lenses, outside our
timescale prior, are not flagged as anomalies by the finite-source checkpoint
($\bmlGullsSubdayFaPct\%$ over threshold) but are read as periodic variables, not as
microlensing; a free-floating-planet-aware model needs sub-day timescales in its prior, not a
threshold change.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------- [D] Discussion paragraph
The most consequential limitation of BinML 1.0 is its input contract of one contiguous season.
\S\ref{sec:gulls:seasons} measures the cost on an independent simulation: a quarter of eligible
events have their peak between seasons, most of them can be scored season by season with
in-season-like recall and lower false alarms, and the planets lost are lost to the 110-day gaps
rather than to the model. A whole-mission model, taking the full 4.7-year light curve, would
recover events spanning seasons and the low-cadence seasons, and would let the real-time
cascade of \S\ref{sec:cascade} run across season boundaries; it requires a mission-length
simulation, detectability labels over the full mission, and a hierarchical input, and is the
natural next version.
